Carbohydrate Counting
Teaching patients with diabetes how to make appropriate food choices (usually by 
means of carbohydrate counting) and using data from blood glucose monitoring to 
evaluate short-term effectiveness are important components of successful nutrition 
Case 1
Deiana is a 64-year-old African American female who has had type 2 diabetes for 
7 years. She retired last year from teaching high school for 30 years. She has experienced 
a difficult past 3 months with the death of her husband of 40 years. She presents at 
the clinic with an A1C of 9.2%. She is very unhappy because her A1C has been under 
7% in the past. She is asking for menus, shopping lists, and any other help she can get 
to improve her eating habits.
APPROACH: Advise Deiana to complete a 3-day food and beverage diary to assess her 
eating patterns and work collaboratively with you to develop a plan for healthy ­eating. 
Refer Deiana to a diabetes self-management education class. Consider referring Deiana 
to a dietitian for a comprehensive nutrition assessment and follow-up counseling as indi-
cated. If these interventions are not successful, carbohydrate counting may be an option.
